analysis.one_liner: Restores the rule that employer health plans must cover birth control without cost-sharing.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in the Senate Health Committee until the Congress ended, despite 38 senators signing on.
analysis.plain_summary: In October 2017, three federal agencies issued rules letting employers with religious or moral objections opt out of the Affordable Care Act's requirement to cover contraceptive services without out-of-pocket charges for their workers. This bill would have wiped those rules out entirely, as if they had never taken effect, so no employer could use them to stop covering birth control. It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who work for employers claiming a religious or moral exemption would keep guaranteed no-cost contraceptive coverage; under the 2017 rules their employers could refuse, forcing women to pay out of pocket or go without.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women whose employers object to coverage

how_it_helps.text: Nullifies the two October 2017 rules that let employers with religious or moral objections drop contraceptive coverage from their health plans, treating them as though they never took effect [S2][S3].
Returns all employer plans to the pre-October-2017 status quo, in which the Affordable Care Act required contraceptive coverage without cost-sharing for their workers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with religious or moral objections, who would lose the ability to opt out, and to a small degree all plan enrollees, whose premiums absorb the cost of covering contraceptive services.

drawbacks.text: The bill was written narrowly to void only the October 13, 2017 interim rules; it would not stop the agencies from issuing new exemption rules with different wording [S3].

Critics of the mandate argue that people who sincerely object should not be forced to arrange coverage they believe violates their conscience; the bill offers no middle-ground accommodation of its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a clean repeal of a specific regulation, so the practical cost is narrow: a modest premium effect and the loss of the exemption for a set of objecting employers, balanced against restoring guaranteed no-cost contraception for their employees.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on October 19, 2017, with 37 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats [S1][S4][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on October 19, 2017; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote afterward [S5].
No Republican senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The two exemption rules the bill targeted were published in the Federal Register on October 13, 2017, six days before the bill was introduced [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with religious or moral objections kept the exemption and could decline to cover contraception for their employees; the rule the bill targeted stayed in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Objecting employers who kept the exemption

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the religious and moral exemption rules and recruited 37 cosponsors.

for.name: 37 Senate Democrats and independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after it was referred: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats, and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.industry: Employers with religious or moral objections
industries.note: The 2017 rules gave these employers a way to drop contraceptive coverage from their plans; the bill would have removed that option, and their workers would have regained no-cost coverage. Because the exemption rules were already in effect, this is a concentrated interest the bill would have taken a benefit away from.

Repealing the exemptions would have restored the requirement that plans cover contraceptive services without cost-sharing, spreading the cost into premiums. Insurers do not profit from the exemptions, and covering preventive care uniformly is a small operational matter for them.
